passage:
I'm Chaitanya, and I was the odd one in that room. Four of us on the shortlist panel, and three had studied at the same engineering college. The candidate was Nirmala, sharp portfolio, from a college none of us knew. Someone said, “She may not fit our style.” Another said, “Rohit is from our place, we know how his batch works.” I said nothing that day. I'm not proud of it.

Afterwards I counted our last five hires: all from two colleges. What we called merit had a lot of comfort in it. Next round I asked, before anyone spoke, “What would we look for if these names weren't on the page?” Nobody argued. Nobody looked at me either. Nirmala got a second interview. I still wonder about the ones who never did.

qa.q: How many of the four panel members had studied at the same engineering college?
qa.a: Three of the four had studied at the same engineering college.

qa.q: Why is Chaitanya not proud of staying silent that day?
qa.a: Chaitanya saw a comfortable bias shaping the choice and did not speak, and that silence let Nirmala's chances shrink.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do in the next round that changed how the panel talked?
qa.a: Chaitanya asked the panel what they would look for if the names were not on the page, before anyone spoke.

qa.q: What was the shortlist meeting like for Nirmala, though Nirmala was not in the room?
qa.a: Nirmala was judged on a college name rather than the portfolio, so a strong application risked being shut out quietly, unseen by Nirmala.

grounding: A panel member notices a hiring panel favouring its own college and quietly asks the panel to look past the names.

passage:
Imran here, from the analytics desk. I sit two desks from Vinita, so I saw how it went. In March she promoted Karthik, who'd studied at her old university. In April she hired two more from there. Then Tessa interviewed, top scores on the test, a degree from somewhere else, and the note said, “Not a culture fit.” I can't tell what Vinita really feels. She's kind, and I think she truly believes she picks the best person.

But three people in a row, same university. I asked whether we could review test scores before the interview chat. She paused, tapped her pen and said, “Maybe. I hadn't seen it that way.” I don't know yet if anything will change.

qa.q: Which university had Karthik studied at?
qa.a: Karthik had studied at Vinita's old university.

qa.q: What might Imran be feeling when asking about reviewing test scores?
qa.a: Imran seems uneasy about the pattern but careful and unsure, since Imran calls Vinita kind and still does not know if anything will change.

qa.q: What small step did Imran suggest that could change how candidates are compared?
qa.a: Imran suggested reviewing test scores before the interview chat, so scores are seen before any feeling of familiarity.

qa.q: How might Vinita see the last three people she chose?
qa.a: Vinita likely sees good people who fit easily, and probably believes each hire was the best on merit without noticing how familiar the background felt.

grounding: An observer at work sees that a colleague who hires and promotes keeps choosing people from her own university and gently asks for a step that widens the view.

passage:
First week in HR: Madhuri processed three new hires for the design team. All three were from Mr Rao's old college in Manipal. She noticed, and told herself it was a coincidence.
Third week: Kalyani, from a small college in Nanded, scored highest on the design test. Mr Rao wrote “not a culture fit” on her form. The next candidate, from Manipal, was hired. Madhuri's stomach turned. Nobody in the office thought it strange. “Rao sir likes people he can trust,” a colleague shrugged.
Fifth week: Madhuri pulled up two years of hiring data and quietly showed her manager. She suggested one simple change: test scores reviewed before names and colleges are seen. Her manager said, “Let's try it next quarter.”

qa.q: Which college were the three new hires from?
qa.a: They were from Mr Rao's old college in Manipal.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when Kalyani was rejected?
qa.a: Her stomach turned; she felt uneasy and troubled by how comfort with the familiar was shutting out a stronger candidate.

qa.q: Why was Madhuri's suggestion a fair way to fix the problem?
qa.a: Reviewing test scores before seeing names and colleges lets merit show first, without accusing Mr Rao directly.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt reading "not a culture fit"?
qa.a: She might feel confused and discouraged, having scored highest, without understanding why she was turned down.

grounding: Shows a young HR worker noticing people being hired from the boss's own college, where comfort with the familiar looks like merit.

passage:
Zeenat, you asked how I got so fussy about interview panels. Let me tell you. I'm Shankar, your old senior, and I once didn't see what was right in front of me.
At twenty-five, at the engineering firm, I noticed something odd. Every promotion that year went to men from our region, who spoke our language at lunch, whose fathers knew each other. I was one of them. I had been promoted too.
One day a woman from the north, Harpreet, who did the best site reports in the office, was passed over again. My boss said, “She's good, but she's not one of us.” He said it so easily.
That night I couldn't sleep. The next week I asked, carefully, why her work wasn't counted. It was the first time I'd asked.

qa.q: Who did the best site reports in the office?
qa.a: Harpreet did the best site reports.

qa.q: How did young Shankar feel after the boss's remark?
qa.a: He felt troubled and uneasy, unable to sleep, realising he himself had benefited from the same bias.

qa.q: What turning point in the story came next?
qa.a: The next week, Shankar carefully asked why Harpreet's work wasn't counted, the first time he questioned it.

qa.q: How might Harpreet have felt being passed over again?
qa.a: She likely felt frustrated and shut out, knowing her work was the best but not being "one of us".

grounding: An elder recalls noticing promotions going only to people from his own region and community, where comfort looked like merit.

passage:
The hospital was hiring a new admin officer, and the panel had thirty minutes for three candidates before the evening OPD rush. Neelam sat beside Dr Thomas, the head of the panel.
The first candidate, from Kochi, had studied at Dr Thomas's old college. They chatted about a teacher they both knew. Dr Thomas smiled the whole time.
The second, Ramya from a small town in Telangana, answered every question clearly, with numbers. Dr Thomas looked at his watch.
The third was rushed through in five minutes.
“The first one,” Dr Thomas said. “Good fit.”
Neelam looked at her notes. Ramya's scores were higher on every line. She took a breath. “Can we compare the scores before deciding? I think Ramya was stronger.”

qa.q: How long did the panel have for the three candidates?
qa.a: The panel had thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling as she looked at her notes?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little nervous, seeing that Ramya scored higher but the familiar candidate was being chosen.

qa.q: Why was asking to compare scores a good step?
qa.a: It brought the discussion back to evidence without accusing Dr Thomas, giving Ramya a fair chance.

qa.q: How might Ramya be affected if the panel had simply followed Dr Thomas?
qa.a: Ramya would have lost a job earned fairly, shut out because she wasn't from a familiar college.

grounding: Shows a young panel member noticing a boss favouring a candidate from his own college, and quietly asking for a fair comparison.

passage:
Gargi had been on the hiring panel at the Bengaluru office for six months before she saw it. Updating the team sheet one evening, she counted: eight people hired this year, six from Varun's college in Pune. Two had first come in as interns through his alumni group.
It hadn't felt like bias in the room. Varun always said things like, "He'll fit right in," or "We speak the same language." Candidates from his college walked in relaxed, joking about the same canteen. Others, like the woman from a Guwahati college last week, answered carefully and got "good, but not quite a fit."
Gargi scrolled back through her notes. The Guwahati candidate had the highest test score of the month.
At the next panel she said, "Can we score the tests before we discuss fit? Our last eight hires are mostly from one place." Varun blinked, then said slowly, "Huh. That's actually true."

qa.q: How many of the eight hires were from Varun's college?
qa.a: Six from Varun's college in Pune.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when she saw the Guwahati candidate's test score?
qa.a: Gargi felt troubled and uneasy, realising a strong candidate had been turned away for a vague "fit".

qa.q: Why is scoring tests before discussing fit a useful step?
qa.a: It puts evidence on the table before comfort with the familiar can sway the panel.

qa.q: What might the Guwahati candidate have experienced in that interview?
qa.a: She may have felt like an outsider among in-jokes, answering carefully and leaving unsure why she was "not quite a fit".

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing that hiring keeps favouring people from the manager's own college, where comfort with the familiar passes for merit.
